Burnout Is When You Have Too Much to Do. Rust-Out Is When Nothing You Do Matters.

We have spent years worrying about burnout. But there is another, quieter problem creeping into corporate life: rust-out. It happens when capable people are not exhausted by their work, but slowly bored out of their ambition.

Procurement is particularly vulnerable. Imagine hiring an experienced professional who understands global markets, negotiates complex contracts, and can challenge entire supply chain strategies — then asking them to spend most of their time chasing approvals, updating spreadsheets, and explaining why a purchase order is still waiting for its seventh signature. The person remains busy, the calendar remains full, and management concludes that everything is working beautifully. Meanwhile, the talent is quietly gathering rust.

The irony is that companies invest millions in digital transformation and AI to improve productivity, yet often preserve the very bureaucracy that prevents their best people from thinking. We automate transactions but rarely redesign the jobs around them.

Burnout makes people want to escape their workload. Rust-out makes them want to escape their potential being wasted. And the most dangerous thing about rust is that, by the time you notice it, the damage has already begun.

Would you sign a contract you never read?

That's exactly what most companies do every time they deploy an AI hiring tool built by someone else. Nobody reads the fine print on how the algorithm actually decides who gets shortlisted.

Regulators have stopped waiting for companies to self-police. New disclosure laws now require businesses to explain why an automated system rejected a candidate not just that it did. "The algorithm decided" is no longer a legal shield, and CEOs who assume it is are carrying risk they don't even know exists.

This isn't a compliance footnote. It's a talent acquisition and brand-trust issue. Candidates talk. A hiring process that quietly filters out strong people for the wrong reasons doesn't just cost you talent it costs you reputation in a market where employer branding is currency.

The leaders getting ahead aren't the ones avoiding AI in recruitment they're the ones asking vendors hard questions before signing: How does this decide? Can you explain a rejection? Who audits it?

If your hiring stack can't answer those questions, you don't have an AI advantage. You have an AI liability.

3️⃣ Nobody Is Watching the Back Door: Just weeks ago, hackers broke into internet-connected supermarket fridges across Europe—turning the heat up to 50°C and ruining millions in stock because nobody was monitoring those connections. Banks are being hit the same way.

Hiring ahead of your systems is a reasonable bet on growth. The exposure sits in what the new hires inherit: no standard terms, no rules for AI tools, and nobody to ask.

So each person makes their own call. A salesperson agrees to uncapped liability to close the quarter. Another signs on the buyer’s paper because the redline queue runs two weeks. A product lead connects a new AI tool to customer data because nobody said not to. Each decision looks reasonable alone. Together they become the contract set that investors’ counsel and enterprise procurement teams review.

The three items on the card are the end state. The order you build them in matters.

First, the contract playbook. Take the clauses your sales team negotiates every week: liability cap, indemnity, data terms, payment terms, and renewal. For each one, write an approved position, a fallback, and the point where the deal comes back to you.

Second, the AI acceptable use policy. List the approved tools and the data each one may touch. Anything off the list needs a named approver.

Third, the governance framework: one owner, a vendor inventory, and a scheduled review of both.

At Altivor, we build all three before the founder becomes the bottleneck.

Most BD hours go on firms that have never paid you.
Your best client has hiring managers you've never met.
Start there.

So here's a sum most owners have never done. All you need is a pen and your fee report.

Take your best client. The one you'd hate to lose. Add up every fee they've paid you since the first placement. Perm, contract margin, all of it.

Now do the same for your next ten clients. One line each.

In a lot of the firms I've been inside, that first number is bigger than the other ten put together. Not always. Often enough that it's worth checking yours.

That gap tells you where your BD hours belong.

Then look at where they actually went last month. I'd bet strangers. Cold calls, LinkedIn, a firm that placed once two years ago and went quiet.

Meanwhile inside your best client you probably know one hiring manager. Maybe two. So who else in there is hiring? Nobody knows, because nobody's asked.

Three things this week. Write down your top five clients by total fees. Next to each, how many hiring managers you actually speak to. Pick one and find out who else is recruiting.

Before you ring their hiring managers, get AI to pull the client's live roles and recent leavers. Then you ring with an actual reason.

Doesn't matter if it's just you or there's twenty of you, the sum works the same.

How many hiring managers do you know inside your best client?

AI and jobs in Ireland: we did some digging, and here's what we think. 🔍

Over the past few weeks at Think Differently, we've been doing our own research into how AI is really affecting hiring. We read the latest ERF Labour Market Monitor, the Government's Digital and AI Strategy, Ibec's reskilling report and a lot of international coverage.

Here's our honest take.

📊 What we're seeing

AI is changing who gets hired, not just how many. ICT roles are down, younger workers are feeling it most, and employers are slower to commit to permanent hires. Contract work is rising, and time to hire is stretching out.
The gap isn't a lack of people. It's a mismatch between the skills employers want and the candidates available. Government analysis suggests up to 63% of Irish jobs are exposed to AI disruption.

🤔 Is the picture accurate?
Mostly, yes. But we'd add three caveats:
1. AI isn't the only factor. Cost pressures, energy prices and general caution are playing a big part too.
2. "AI" can be a convenient label. We've seen profitable global companies cut a fifth of their staff in the name of AI while buying back their own shares. Not every cut blamed on AI is really about AI.
3. Much of the data is sentiment, not hard numbers. Useful for trends, but not the full story.

⚖️ Is enough being done?
In our view: good intentions, thin delivery.
✅ Ireland has a national AI strategy, a skills observatory and a free AI skills platform aiming to reach one million people. That's a real start.
❌ But the early courses are aimed at older adults, farmers, sole traders and people returning to work. Very little targets the professionals most exposed right now: marketing, comms, admin and early career talent.
❌ Women and younger workers are expected to be hit hardest, yet there's little support aimed specifically at them.
❌ There's nothing stopping companies from using AI as cover for cuts made purely for margin.
To be fair, Ireland relies heavily on multinational investment, so there's a real balancing act between protecting workers and staying attractive to business. It's early days. But the pace of change is fast, and policy needs to catch up.

💡 Where we stand
We use technology to work smarter, but people make the decisions. Every time. Candidates have told us that's what they want, and we agree.

For employers: AI won't fix a broken hiring process. Move quickly on great people, and think about reskilling your team before replacing them.

For candidates: build your AI skills, stay curious, and don't rule out contract roles. They're often the door in.

We'd love to hear what you're seeing. Is AI changing how your team hires? Drop a comment or get in touch. ☕



This piece reflects Think Differently's own opinion, based on publicly available research including the ERF Q3 2026 Labour Market Monitor.

🔮 What will recruitment look like in 2027? The talent landscape is changing faster than ever.
As we look ahead, one thing is becoming increasingly clear: the next wave of technology growth will bring an entirely new set of hiring challenges.

Here are five trends we believe will shape recruitment over the coming year:

1. AI talent will go beyond traditional engineering.
Demand for AI infrastructure engineers, LLM specialists, agentic AI developers and AI product leaders is set to grow as businesses move from experimentation to real-world implementation.
2. FinTech will need more than financial expertise.
The evolution of digital payments, embedded finance, stablecoins and financial infrastructure will create demand for professionals combining finance, technology and regulatory knowledge.
3. Web3 and crypto hiring will become more specialised.
As institutional adoption develops, blockchain infrastructure, smart contract security, digital asset compliance and institutional business development will become increasingly important talent areas.
4. Skills will matter more than job titles.
Companies will increasingly look beyond traditional CVs and academic qualifications, prioritising practical experience, adaptability and the ability to work with emerging technologies.
5. The demand for hybrid talent will grow.
The most valuable professionals may be those who combine technical expertise with commercial thinking, leadership, communication and an understanding of business.

📌 What does this mean for recruitment?
Finding talent is no longer simply about matching a CV to a job description. It's about understanding where industries are heading, identifying emerging skill sets and building relationships with people who can help businesses stay ahead.

We're focused on connecting ambitious businesses with specialist talent across AI, FinTech, Web3, Blockchain, Crypto and emerging technology.

Your LinkedIn profile, posts, projects, GitHub, certifications and professional network can all contribute to your visibility.

NVIDIA lost its founder. Intel may have gained an opening.
Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO yesterday. Elon Musk says hiring him would be an honor and the internet is already writing his Terafab job description.
Fun, but I think the bigger story is elsewhere. Nvidia hasn’t lost Taiwan: orders and packaging capacity are settled for the next 1 to 1.5 years. It still holds roughly 70% of the AI chip market. 
And the alternatives buyers are turning to come out of the same place, since TSMC fabricates chips for all five hyperscalers and Broadcom. Switching chip brands reshuffles the queue. It doesn’t add supply.
That’s Intel's opening. It’s the only American company attempting leading-edge manufacturing and its 14A process just hit the design-kit milestone customers use to start designs. Apple, AMD and NVIDIA are reportedly evaluating it and even Terafab reportedly plans to use it.
What Intel needs:
One named anchor customer.
Packaging as the easy way in.
Customer prepayments that fund capacity before it exists, the way Huang’s long-term contracts did for his suppliers.
Intel doesn’t need the man. It needs his method.
The risk is real: 14A isn’t expected to be production-ready until 2027.
Who signs first?

A GPU operator's sales team may end up determining how much of the next cluster its founders still own. The customer contract helps shape the debt conversation long before the machines start earning their keep.

Matt Ballensweig and Leon Marshall are building Marble around that connection. The co-founders and co-CEOs announced an $11M Seed round on November 10, led by Polychain Capital, with Maven 11, Ripple, Susquehanna Crypto, Lattice Ventures, Blockwall and other investors participating.

Ballensweig previously led institutional trading at BitGo. Marshall ran Galaxy's European business. Their new firm brings 2 developing businesses together: Marble Compute, focused on private credit for independent GPU operators and neoclouds, and Marble Markets, focused on institutional trading across digital assets, real-world assets, prediction markets and compute.

For the GPU operator, the financing discussion reaches well beyond the equipment invoice. Marble plans to evaluate the hardware, the customers committed to renting its capacity and the operator's ability to repay. A buyer's creditworthiness and contract duration become part of the argument for how much debt the business can support.

That gives the sales contract a second audience. The AI customer needs capacity it can rely on. The lender needs to understand the payments expected from that customer. The operator sits between them, trying to fund a build without putting every expansion dollar on its own equity tab.

Marble's planned compute forwards would let operators agree today on pricing for future capacity. Together with its proposed credit business, that creates a route for sales, hedging and financing to inform one another. It also requires people who can underwrite the customer relationship as carefully as the hardware.

Marble is hiring across underwriting, structuring, risk, engineering, trading and operations. Those jobs will have to agree on the same transaction.

These remain planned offerings. Marble's product pages say no services are currently offered, and regulatory-dependent products remain subject to the required approvals. The seed finances the firm being built, rather than establishing that lenders have already funded GPU customers.

For an independent operator preparing another cluster, Marble is bringing the prospective lender into a conversation that starts with whoever will buy the compute. That leaves the sales team with another reason to care about the terms it signs.

A quick public service announcement for LinkedIn’s search algorithm, the recruitment industry, and enterprise hiring managers:

A Fixed-Term Contract (FTC) is not a "Contract" role. Grouping them under the same search filter is creating a massive inefficiency in the market.

Right now, I am seeing a huge surge in organisations trying to secure transient, highly specialised skills through 12-month FTCs rather than outside-IR35 B2B contracts, or even inside-IR35 roles. It highlights a fundamental misunderstanding of why the independent consulting market exists.

The Economics of Specialism:
When an enterprise brings in a senior interim leader or specialist, they are buying agility and immediate impact. They are paying for someone to parachute in, solve a complex delivery or governance crisis, and cleanly exit.
As professional contractors, we operate as independent businesses. We provision our own holiday pay, our own pensions, our own health insurance, and our own training. We don't need a gym pass or a company wellness day. What we do need is the commercial day rate that covers those self-funded provisions. What the business needs is the ability to rapidly onboard and offboard capability without dragging us through heavy HR payroll processes or getting trapped in a 3-month notice period.

The IR35 Elephant in the Room:
Let’s be honest about the root cause of this surge. It is heavily driven by a corporate reluctance—or outright fear—of conducting proper IR35 status determinations. Wrapping a role in an FTC is often used as a convenient, zero-risk workaround to avoid dealing with the legislation entirely. But that administrative "convenience" comes at a steep price: you instantly lock out the top tier of independent specialists who refuse to operate as disguised, heavily-taxed temporary employees.

An FTC is just temporary employment. It carries all the friction, HR overhead, and rigidity of a permanent hire, but with an expiration date.

If a business needs a temporary employee to cover maternity leave, an FTC is perfect. But if you need an independent specialist to architect a transformation, deliver a £100M+ programme, or govern a high-risk AI deployment, you have to engage them commercially.

Agility has a specific commercial vehicle. Let’s stop mixing them up.

⚡ Streaming every raw PLC and BMS tag straight to the cloud is an expensive mistake.

When companies start their Industry 4.0 or smart building journey, the instinct is simple: 
“Connect the gateway, push 10,000 tags every second to AWS IoT, and build dashboards.”

Within months, three problems hit: 
❌ Cloud ingestion and storage bills skyrocket 
❌ Network dropouts cause blind spots in critical telemetry 
❌ Latency makes real-time operational response impossible

After 8+ years building Edge-to-Cloud solutions across industrial automation and BMS environments, here is the rule I follow for where data should live:
1. Keep at the Edge (Linux Gateways / Python / Local Controllers):
    • High-frequency polling & filtering: Read Modbus/BACnet registers locally at millisecond intervals, filter out noise, and publish only on change (Report by Exception) or aggregated intervals.
    • Local buffering (Store-and-Forward): If the WAN drops, the edge gateway caches telemetry locally and backfills cleanly once connectivity returns—zero data loss.
    • Immediate safety & local logic: Closed-loop responses and local alarming must never depend on a round-trip to the cloud.

2. Send to the Cloud (AWS IoT / Enterprise Analytics):
    • Multi-site benchmarking: Comparing chiller plant COP, OEE, or energy intensity across multiple facilities in Dubai, Abu Dhabi, and Sharjah.
    • Long-term historical trends & AI/ML: Training predictive maintenance models on months of clean, normalized operational data.
    • Enterprise integration: Feeding verified KPIs into ERP, CMMS, and sustainability reporting platforms.

The takeaway: The edge gives you resilience and speed; the cloud gives you scale and intelligence. Great IIoT architecture uses both in balance.

How are you splitting your workloads between the edge and the cloud right now? 👇

The promise that AI takes the routine and leaves people the judgment holds for 22% of advertised jobs, by the count in PwC's 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer.
​
In 52%, it runs the other way: AI takes the expert part of the work.
​
In the report's examples, AI screens a recruiter's CVs and leaves the contract negotiations to the recruiter. For an inventory clerk, it manages the inventory and leaves the clerk to move the stock.
​
Both kinds of job are highly exposed to AI. The remaining 26% of advertised jobs have low exposure.
​
So how exposed a job is doesn't tell you which way it goes. What tells you is which part of the work AI takes.
​
Job postings already show the difference. In the six countries PwC has long-run data for, postings grew 39% from 2018 to 2025 where AI takes the basic part, and 17% where it takes the expert part. Advertised salaries since 2021 are up 37% and 26%, in the same order.
​
PwC calls jobs where AI takes the expert part "democratised", and I think the word explains the numbers. When AI does the part that took years to learn, more people can do the job. When AI does the part anyone could do, the years are what you're hiring for.
​
Closer to our industry, PwC's chart places finance managers and credit and loans officers on the side where AI reduces the expertise required. Valuers and loss assessors are among its examples of jobs where the expert part stays with people.
​
PwC's advice to leaders is to consider how AI is changing the expertise each role needs before investing in talent and skills. I'd put it as one question per role: once AI does what it does well, what's left, the expert part or the remainder?
​
The answer decides who you hire into the role and what you train the people already in it to do.
​

Anthropic's S-1 has 88 risk factors: 46 on business and industry, 12 on privacy, cybersecurity and intellectual property, 9 on governance structure, 8 on ownership of Class A common stock, 7 on tax and accounting matters and 6 on legal and regulatory matters. This series goes through each one, in the order they are presented in the first public S-1 filing (26 Oct 2026), to discuss the possible mitigations for the risk described.

Risk factor 37 says weak customer support could hurt subscriptions, "particularly with respect to our enterprise customers" (p. 83). Support includes "hands-on technical implementation, customization, and solution engineering support" (p. 82).

Support is the expansion engine. The growth model "depends significantly on driving deeper adoption and expanded use cases within our existing customer base." Without support, customers may limit usage, fail to renew at expected levels or reduce spend (p. 83). The strain comes from winning. There is "no assurance" of hiring enough support personnel, "particularly if our sales exceed our internal forecasts" (p. 83).

The risk factor discloses no mitigation. Elsewhere, the filing answers with leverage. Applied AI teams "embed more deeply with select customers" (p. 201). The Claude Frontier Academy, backed by a $100 million commitment, aims to train 10,000 engineers by the end of 2027 (p. 202). Ode with Anthropic, an AI services company formed with private equity firms, is set up to support mid-sized companies "over the long term" (p. 202). The rest leans on partners and the customer's own engineers. Investors should ask what share of revenue the Applied AI teams cover.

Support can also change by choice. Decisions balancing stockholders, affected stakeholders and the Company Purpose may include "changes in how we deliver customer support" (p. 113). The risk factor also flags support "in languages other than English" and "across expanded time zones" (p. 83).

For Clients, the fix is the contract: severity levels, response times, escalation path, hours in your time zone and language. If a partner deploys Claude, get in writing who answers the first call. Train your own engineers so production never waits in a vendor's queue.

Autonomous AI agents are moving from demos into daily operations. The question for leaders is no longer whether they work, but where they should be allowed to act on their own.

A useful way to decide is to grade every task by two things: how reversible the action is and how costly a mistake would be. Agents can run freely on work that is low cost and easy to undo, such as drafting, research and data clean-up. They should recommend, not act, where mistakes are expensive or permanent, such as payments, contracts and hiring.

Start narrow, measure the error rate, and widen the agent's authority only as the evidence builds.

One of the most formative periods of my career was my time at RusselSmith.

I joined when the company was in its early stages of evolution. I remember coming out of one of those final interviews that makes you question whether you've actually secured the job. But I did! 🎉

I was only three years into my career, and it turned out to be the kind of hire where the leadership team saw more than my existing competence. They recognised my character, potential, curiosity and willingness to learn.

𝗔𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗮 𝗷𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘆 𝗶𝘁 𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗯𝗲! ❤️

I progressed through different roles and departments, working across business development, commercial operations, sales, financial planning, project management, business intelligence and strategy. As the company evolved from its early stages into a mid-sized business, I had the opportunity to grow alongside it.

I built close relationships with the executive leadership team, reporting on contract performance, business and offshore operations, managing transformation projects and providing insights and recommendations to support commercial decisions.

It was an incredibly exciting period of learning, creativity and taking on unfamiliar challenges. Along the way, I was fortunate to receive several awards, including the RusselSmith ACE Award, Cross-Functional Award and HSE Safety Person of the Year.🏆

But beyond the titles, promotions and awards, what I valued most was the trust, the freedom to contribute to a constantly evolving company, the people and the relationships that remain with me today.

𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗜 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝗚𝗲𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘆...

The organisation supported me in continuing to work remotely, recognising that building a family was also important to me. This was long before COVID made remote working commonplace. That level of trust and support meant a great deal!

Today, RusselSmith has evolved into Arridex, reflecting its continued growth into a broader industrial technology group. 

𝗔𝗻𝗱 𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲'𝘀 𝘀𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗜 𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗸 𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸:

Today, we're discussing the future of work, AI, changing skill requirements and what organisations should look for when hiring.

Technical competence matters, but so do curiosity, integrity, adaptability, character and the willingness to keep learning.

From recognising potential beyond a CV to embracing remote working before it became mainstream, perhaps RusselSmith was already ahead of its time.

Now, that's what I call visionary leadership! ✨

Remote jobs are not gone. You are just searching the wrong words.

I use Perplexity to find global remote jobs that normal filters miss.

A lot of companies do not say:
“work from anywhere”

They use other words like:
• contract
• freelance
• global team
• work across time zones
• anywhere
• outside the US
• remote in selected countries

That small change matters.

Here is the simple workflow:

1/ Search for hiring signs
In Perplexity, prompt:

“Find companies hiring for [your role] that may accept people from many countries. Look for words like contract, freelance, global team, work across time zones, anywhere, or outside the US. Skip jobs that clearly need US-only hiring. Show me the company, job link, country limits, job type, and why it may fit.”

Now you are not only searching “remote.”
You are searching how companies really write it.

2/ Check the company pages
Then ask:

“Check company career pages, founder posts, and hiring pages for this role. Find companies that look open to global remote workers, even if the job title does not say work from anywhere.”

This helps you find jobs filters miss.

3/ Save the good ones
Put the results into Notion or Google Sheets.

Track:
• company
• role
• link
• country limit
• time zone need
• job type
• notes

4/ Match your CV to that kind of job
Use ChatGPT or Claude.
Ask it to rewrite your best CV points for:
• working alone
• clear writing
• fast work
• working with people in different time zones
• real results

The best global remote jobs are often not under the “remote” filter.
They are hidden behind simple words.

AI helps you find them faster.
